The Supreme Court struck it down in 2015 as unconstitutional. The text remains printed in the official edition, but the Commission never took effect. The collegium of judges continues to make the recommendations.
124B: This article lists the functions of the National Judicial Appointments Commission. It was to recommend persons for appointment as Chief Justice of India and Judges of the Supreme Court. It was also to recommend Chief Justices and Judges of the High Courts, and their transfers. The Commission was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015 before it could work.
124C: This article would have let Parliament regulate the appointment procedure for judges by law. It belongs to the National Judicial Appointments Commission scheme of the 99th Amendment. The Supreme Court struck that scheme down in 2015. No such law has been made.
131A: This article no longer exists. It had given the Supreme Court exclusive jurisdiction over questions about the constitutional validity of Central laws. The 43rd Amendment omitted it in 1978. High Courts regained their ordinary jurisdiction in such matters. The omission restored the position that existed before the 42nd Amendment made the change.
134A: This article creates the certificate for appeal. A High Court may grant it on its own motion, and a party may also apply for it. The certificate is what articles 132, 133, and 134 require. It opens the door to the Supreme Court.
139A: This article lets the Supreme Court unify cases. Where the same question of law is pending before the Supreme Court and one or more High Courts, the cases may be transferred and heard together. The Court may act on its own motion or on an application. It may also transfer a case from one High Court to another for the ends of justice.
144A: This article no longer exists. It had required a special bench when the Court decided questions about the constitutional validity of Central or State laws. The 43rd Amendment omitted it in 1978. The ordinary bench arrangements now govern such cases.
228A: This article no longer exists. It had set special rules for State High Courts deciding questions about the constitutional validity of State laws. The 43rd Amendment omitted it in 1978. The ordinary jurisdiction of the High Courts was restored after that. The omission returned such cases to the ordinary bench.
239A: This article lets Parliament create legislatures for Union territories. Parliament may by law create a legislature for Puducherry, elected or partly nominated. It may also create a Council of Ministers for the territory. Such a law is not treated as an amendment of the Constitution under article 368. Puducherry today has an elected Assembly under this article.
239AA: This article gives Delhi its special constitutional scheme. The National Capital Territory has a Legislative Assembly chosen by direct election. It can make laws on the State List and the Concurrent List, except public order, police, and land. It has a Council of Ministers of not more than ten per cent of the Assembly's strength, collectively responsible to the Assembly. Parliament's law prevails where its own laws collide with the Assembly's.
239AB: This article covers a breakdown in Delhi’s government. The President must first be satisfied that the administration cannot be carried on under article 239AA. The President may then suspend its provisions by order. The Assembly is suspended. The President assumes its powers for the period. This is the President’s rule provision for Delhi.
268A: This article no longer exists. It had provided for service tax levied by the Union and collected and shared with the States. The 101st Amendment omitted it in 2016. The Goods and Services Tax replaced the whole arrangement. Article 268 next to it still governs stamp duties.
329A: This article no longer exists. It had made special provision for elections to Parliament in the case of the Prime Minister and the Speaker. It belongs to the Emergency era. The 44th Amendment omitted it in 1978. The ordinary election law applies to all candidates alike.
334A: This article controls when the women's reservation under the 106th Amendment takes effect. The reservation covers the Lok Sabha, the state assemblies, and the Delhi assembly. It comes into effect after a delimitation done for this purpose, following the relevant census figures. Reserved seats continue till the date Parliament fixes by law. Rotation follows each later delimitation. Until then, existing representation is not disturbed.
359A: This article no longer exists. It had applied the emergency provisions of Part XVIII to the State of Punjab. That was during the disturbance of the late 1980s. The 63rd Amendment omitted it in 1990. The general emergency provisions now govern every State alike.
371B: This article gives Assam a special provision. The President may by order provide for a committee of the State's Legislative Assembly. The committee is constituted in a way that gives representation to the tribal areas of the State. It considers and reports on matters of interest to those areas.
371D: This article gives Andhra Pradesh and Telangana their special provisions. The President may by order provide equitable opportunities in public employment and in education across the State. The order may organise posts and admissions by zones or local areas. It may also set up an Administrative Tribunal to hear service matters. The article was made for the Andhra Pradesh reorganisation and now serves both States.
371F: This article sets Sikkim's special provisions after it joined India in 1975. The Legislative Assembly of Sikkim has not less than thirty members. Sikkim keeps one seat in the Lok Sabha. Existing laws and courts continue subject to adaptation. Property rights and old customs are protected as the article provides.
